idiom_name: Equatable/Comparable conformances with synthesised requirements and protocol-extension default operators
implementation_notes: This is the pattern absorbed into the language: Comparable requires only < (plus == from Equatable) and the standard library supplies >, <= and >= in a protocol extension, so conformance alone donates the relational family to every member. For structs whose stored properties are Equatable and for enums without associated values the compiler synthesises Equatable (and Hashable), and an enum with Comparable payloads can be declared Comparable to get ordering by case declaration order and then lexicographically by payload (SE-0185, SE-0266). Write the operators yourself only when the semantics differ from the member-wise default - a normalised date, a key projection - and prefer protocol conformance over free operator functions, because only conformance makes the type usable with generic algorithms such as sorted(), min() and Comparable-constrained APIs.
pitfalls: Conformance must be declared in the type's own declaration or a same-file extension for synthesis to apply, and a hand-written == takes precedence over the synthesised one, so the two can diverge unnoticed.
The protocol's default <=, > and >= are defined in terms of <, so an inconsistent < (not a strict total order) propagates to every operator at once.

Operator requirements are static members: for classes the comparison cannot be overridden dynamically, and comparing base-typed values compares only the base state - value types or a class hierarchy with hand-written equality are safer.
